problem: Deep-RL visual (object-goal) navigation agents need many training scenes annotated with object information, and they transfer poorly to new environments. Existing unsupervised or meta-RL methods either need many hand-designed meta-training tasks or use heuristic intrinsic rewards (curiosity, DIAYN) that do not produce skills useful for visual navigation.
motivation: Building and annotating many 3D environments is expensive, so the paper studies a low-resource setting: many unannotated scenes and only a few annotated ones. Humans solve new tasks quickly by reusing motor primitives learned elsewhere. This suggests learning task-agnostic meta-skills (bypass obstacles, go straight, turn) without supervision and then learning only a small task-specific controller.
key_idea: A task generator and a hierarchical meta-learner are trained adversarially on unannotated scenes. The generator proposes a curriculum of increasingly hard and diverse image-goal navigation tasks. The meta-learner learns shared sub-policies (meta-skills) via Reptile. For object navigation, only a new master policy that selects among the frozen sub-policies is trained on a few annotated scenes.
insight: Two things drive the gains: (1) a curriculum of automatically generated tasks, and (2) keeping the transferable part (the sub-policies) separate from a per-task master policy, which is re-initialized for each task. In Table 2, removing the adversarial curriculum (random-location targets instead) cuts SR from 27.74 to 20.23. Removing the hierarchy (plain LSTM-A3C updated on each task) gives 24.27 SR / 10.54 SPL, and removing the Reptile meta-update gives 23.57 / 11.03. Plain pre-training on image-goal navigation with a random or hand-crafted curriculum generator barely helps A3C (19.73 and 20.57 SR vs 19.20). So the transfer comes from the meta-learned hierarchical skills, not from exposure to image-driven navigation itself. The benefit is largest on long episodes (L≥5: SR 20.57 vs 10.31 for Curiosity). Visualized sub-policies behave consistently across scenes (go straight while bypassing obstacles, turn right, turn left).
method:
Curriculum-based adversarial task generator:
  - The generator policy starts at s0, takes actions and stops at sT.
  - It sends its egocentric observation oT as an image goal; the meta-learner must reach sT from s0 (image-driven navigation with target x, y and viewing angle).
  - Generator reward: R_G = k(1−r) − λn + η·ΣΣ KL(π'(·|s_t) || π(·|s_t)), where r is the meta-learner's success rate after multiple episodes, n is the number of generator steps (a step penalty that yields the easiest task the learner cannot yet solve), and the KL term is a diversity bonus against the 4 most recent previous generator policies.

Shared hierarchical policy (MLSH-style):
  - A task-specific master policy φ picks one of K sub-policies θ={θ1..θK}.
  - The chosen sub-policy executes a fixed N primitive actions before control returns to the master.
  - φ is re-initialized per task; θ is shared across all tasks.

Meta-RL update:
  - For each generated task, a warm-up period of W episodes trains only the master policy with A3C, with sub-policies frozen.
  - A joint period of J episodes then updates both φ and a copy θ̃.
  - The shared sub-policies are updated with a Reptile step θ ← θ + β(θ̃ − θ), with (θ − θ̃) treated as a gradient in SGD.

Transfer to semantic visual navigation:
  - Sub-policies are frozen and a new master policy is trained with A3C on 20 annotated scenes.
  - Master input is the egocentric RGB observation plus the word embedding of the target object.
  - Reward is a positive final reward for reaching the target within a step limit and a negative per-step reward.
Number of sub-policies: K=7 is chosen from an ablation (Fig. 5). SR and SPL rise from 4 to 7 sub-policies; with more, SPL drops because too many sub-policies cause confusion.

setting.backbone: LSTM-A3C hierarchical policy (master policy + 7 sub-policies), trained from scratch; task generator is a separate RL policy
setting.training_data: 60 unannotated AI2-THOR scenes for unsupervised meta-training on self-generated image-goal tasks (no object labels or navigation rewards); then 20 annotated AI2-THOR scenes for supervised A3C training of the master policy (low-resource setting)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + target object word embedding (image goal from the task generator during meta-training)
setting.action_space: 6 discrete actions: MoveAhead, RotateLeft, RotateRight, LookDown, LookUp, Done (sub-policies execute N-step chunks)

numbers.backbone: LSTM-A3C hierarchical policy (7 sub-policies), trained from scratch
numbers.extra: Custom AI2-THOR split: 60 unannotated scenes for unsupervised meta-training; the other 60 split into 20 train / 20 val / 20 test. Target object classes follow SAVN. SR_L5/SPL_L5 = episodes with optimal path length ≥5. Not directly comparable to SAVN's split.

results: On the 20 unseen AI2-THOR test scenes, ULTRA reaches 27.74 SR / 11.47 SPL. It beats the strongest baseline, Curiosity (21.07 / 8.51), as well as A3C from scratch (19.20 / 7.48; +53.34% relative SPL) and DIAYN (17.23 / 6.30). On long episodes (L≥5) it roughly doubles SR (20.57 vs 10.31 for Curiosity), and it converges in about one-third of the baselines' iterations.
limitations: Small-scale evaluation on single-room AI2-THOR scenes with a custom 60/20/20/20 scene split. Numbers are not directly comparable to SAVN or later ObjectNav benchmarks, and absolute success is low (27.74% SR).
Sub-policies run for a fixed N steps and are frozen at test time. Only a few coarse motor primitives emerge (go straight, turn right, turn left), and too many sub-policies hurt SPL.

The meta-training task (image-goal navigation from a fixed start) differs from the target task. The paper shows plain image-goal pre-training does not transfer, and there are no real-robot or larger-environment experiments.
compares_to: DIAYN + MAML (unsupervised meta-RL, Gupta et al.)
